rationale: Start with a broad gradient ending at high organic to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded central cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well within 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent gradient shallowing if needed.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map selectivity across the available temperature range. This will show whether cooling separates the central cluster and late doublet more effectively than heating.

Retain the promising low temperature and make the gradient shallower to improve the two remaining critical pairs. The current last peak at 6.06 minutes leaves substantial room to gain resolution before incurring a time penalty.

Raise the starting organic fraction while retaining the shallow gradient and low temperature. This tests a new selectivity lever for the remaining close pair and should bring the late peaks earlier, preserving room below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Test a small temperature increase at the best gradient, since the critical central pair appears to change elution order as the gradient becomes shallower. This may improve its selectivity while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Use a shallower gradient to move beyond the central pair's apparent elution-order crossover, while the higher starting organic fraction limits retention time. Returning to 25 C should protect the neighboring pair that became critical at 30 C.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. The minimum resolution of 1.93 provides some margin, while injection 7 remains the benchmark.

Raise starting organic by one step to bring the peaks earlier while slightly reducing gradient slope. The gentler slope may preserve the critical pair's resolution, which has little margin in injection 8.

Combine a slightly shallower gradient with a 5 C temperature increase to recover resolution of the central pair at the higher starting organic fraction. This may retain full resolution while eluting the last peak earlier than injection 8.

Shallow the gradient at injection 10's settings to lift the remaining critical pair toward baseline resolution. Its 7.38-minute last peak leaves room to gain separation while potentially remaining faster than injection 8.

Lower temperature one step to separate the late doublet that became critical in injection 11 and improve spacing ahead of the central cluster. The shallow gradient may preserve central-pair resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate gradient slope at 30 C to balance the central separations without compressing the late doublet as much as injection 11. The lower starting organic fraction may recover central-pair resolution while delivering a faster fully resolved run.

With maximum-score methods secured, test whether a shallower gradient at 60 C can resolve the crowded peaks seen in injection 2. This explores a different selectivity regime that could yield a faster fully resolved method.

Lengthen the high-temperature gradient by one step to improve the sole remaining critical pair. This could achieve full resolution with the last peak still earlier than the fastest maximum-score method so far.

Use a slope slightly steeper than injection 14 to improve its late critical pair while retaining sufficient central-cluster resolution. Adjusting the endpoint gives an intermediate slope unavailable through a two-minute duration step alone.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the late critical pair above 1.5 while preserving the central separations. The gradient should still extend beyond the last peak, so the lower endpoint should not affect elution.

Shift the organic window upward one step while preserving injection 17's gradient slope to seek earlier elution. This tests whether the faster window retains the three close pairs; injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Shallow the gradient at the higher starting organic fraction to recover the two central separations lost in injection 18. The later pairs have some resolution margin, so this may restore full resolution while remaining faster than injection 17.

Test a one-step temperature reduction to change selectivity of the two remaining close pairs without further shallowing the gradient, which improves one but worsens the other. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the fastest confirmed fully resolved conditions and increase gradient slope slightly, from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute. This tests the faster-elution boundary while retaining injection 17 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction restores central-pair selectivity enough to permit a steeper, shorter gradient. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if this tradeoff reduces resolution below 1.5.
Test one duration step below the fastest fully resolved low-temperature method to establish its speed boundary. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method overall.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower slope to seek a faster fully resolved high-temperature method. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed method achieving the maximum CRF.

Use a gradient slope between the two confirmed fully resolved low-temperature runs to target maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 8 and earlier elution than injection 7. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.
